definition: Submissive means readily yielding to another's authority or will — letting your own judgment give way and obeying without resistance.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word submissive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know submissive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The once-blunt negotiator turned oddly submissive whenever the chairman entered, conceding terms she had rejected an hour earlier.
Deferential is milder than submissive: a deferential junior yields politely out of respect while keeping a will of her own, but a submissive one lets that will give way altogether.

Servile goes further than submissive: submission surrenders your judgment when authority presses, while servility adds eager, fawning self-abasement — the flattery volunteered before anyone even asks.

Compliant means going along with rules, requests, and procedures — you comply with a policy, a deadline, a doctor's orders. Submissive is about persons, not paperwork: it describes a will bowing to someone's authority, often against the yielder's own judgment, even when nothing has actually been asked.

Docile means naturally mild and easily led — a docile temperament simply has no fight in it to begin with. Submissive describes the yielding itself, in the moment: a strong-willed person with plenty of fight can still turn submissive when authority stares them down.

Reviewers later called the committee remiss for approving the bridge design after a single afternoon's discussion.
Submissive means readily yielding to another's authority or will — letting your own judgment give way and obeying without resistance.
Everyone at the pass could see the head chef had misread the ticket — table nine had ordered the salmon.
The new line cook opened his mouth, caught the chef's glare, and closed it again.
He plated the wrong dish exactly as directed, apologized for a delay that was not his fault, and asked, quietly, whether the chef would like the garnish changed too.
Three months in, the kitchen had taught him to be submissive: whatever he knew, authority outranked it.
The cook has judgment of his own — he knows the ticket was misread — but he lets it collapse the moment authority pushes back, obeying without resistance.
That surrender of one's own will to another's is exactly what submissive describes.
disapproving to neutral; usually implies a will that ought to push back
Submissive takes 'to' ('submissive to the board') and almost always carries a raised eyebrow: it suggests the yielding goes further than it should.

Keep it apart from cooperative, which shares work rather than surrendering will, and from this unit's impassive, which hides feeling behind a still face — an impassive negotiator may be yielding nothing at all.
And do not confuse the adjective with the verb's paperwork sense: an essay is submitted, never submissive.

In her memoir, violinist Elena Brandt lingers on a puzzle from her first season: the concertmaster, Viktor, a man who had argued with every conductor in Europe.
Under the celebrated maestro Osei, Viktor became, in her word, submissive.
He accepted bowings he privately called backwards and dynamics he had mocked at dinner.
He raised no objection in rehearsal.
When Osei glanced his way, Viktor simply nodded and marked the change into his part.
Brandt is careful to note what this was not.
It was not laziness, and it was not agreement; his own judgment, voiced freely elsewhere, went silent in the hall.
The puzzle, she writes, was watching a strong will set itself down at the door like a coat, every single morning.
